scope: Eleven additions to the existing Behavior Chain and Solution Analysis entry. Original educational adaptations, not a treatment program.
metadata_note: The public schema has no example_user_queries field. These editorial retrieval examples are kept here rather than adding unsupported frontmatter.
source_verification: Specific linked skill pages and Linehan teaching notes were checked during authoring. No source worksheet text is reproduced.

patterns.title: STOP: Create Space Before Acting
patterns.short_description: Interrupt an automatic reaction, notice what is happening, and choose a next action that serves your goals.
example_user_queries: I keep replying before I have time to think.
How can I pause before sending a message I might regret?
I notice anger only when I am already talking sharply.
I want a moment to choose what to do next.
I react quickly when I feel criticized.
How do I interrupt an escalating conversation?
I need a brief pause without ignoring the problem.
I want to slow down between an urge and an action.

visual_decision.reading: An ink line approaches a pause marked by two bars. A separated green segment resumes toward a small node, expressing a chosen next action after interruption rather than an automatic continuation.

patterns.title: Wise Mind: Bringing Feelings and Facts Together
patterns.short_description: Make room for emotional experience and practical information together before choosing a response that fits what matters.
example_user_queries: My feelings and my practical plans seem to pull in opposite directions.
I keep arguing with myself about a decision.
I dismiss my feelings and then regret the choice.
I want to consider facts without losing what matters to me.
I feel pressured to choose before I understand what I want.
How can I listen to both my worry and the practical constraints?
I cannot find a perfect answer and need a reasonable next step.
I want to make room for uncertainty in a decision.

visual_decision.reading: Two overlapping outlines retain their distinct edges. A green center marks the shared area, expressing emotional and reasonable perspectives brought together without one erasing the other.

patterns.title: Identify and Describe Emotions: Understand the Sequence
patterns.short_description: Describe an emotional episode by distinguishing its context, interpretations, sensations, urges, expressions, and aftereffects.
example_user_queries: I know I feel bad but I cannot tell what the feeling is.
I seem to feel several emotions at once.
I want to understand what happened emotionally during a conversation.
I confuse what I wanted to do with what I actually did.
I get upset about being upset.
How can I describe a feeling without judging myself?
I cannot remember which feeling came first.
I want to distinguish a body sensation from an interpretation.

visual_decision.reading: Four separate ink and gray elements sit along a loose sequence. An accented element marks a named component. The gaps preserve distinctions among an event, experience, urge, and action without implying a fixed causal order.

patterns.title: Check the Facts: Examine the Story Around the Feeling
patterns.short_description: Separate what you observed from what you inferred, consider uncertainty, and reassess how an emotion fits the situation.
example_user_queries: I assume a short message means someone is angry with me.
I am treating a prediction as if it already happened.
How do I separate what I know from what I fear?
I need to examine a concern without dismissing my feelings.
I cannot tell whether my interpretation fits the evidence.
I keep imagining the worst after an ambiguous comment.
I want a more accurate assessment even if uncertainty remains.
How can I check whether there is a real problem to address?

visual_decision.reading: A single ink observation branches toward three outlined possibilities. One green return connector highlights comparing possibilities with the observation, rather than automatically selecting a comforting interpretation.

patterns.title: DEAR MAN: Make a Clear Request or Say No
patterns.short_description: Prepare a clear request or refusal, explain what matters, and stay focused while considering workable options.
example_user_queries: I keep hinting instead of asking clearly.
I agree to things before considering my capacity.
How can I say no without overexplaining?
I need to ask for a change to an arrangement.
I lose my point when someone pushes back.
I want to prepare a clear boundary statement.
I need to ask for help while feeling nervous.
How can I discuss alternatives without giving up my limit?

visual_decision.reading: Four ink strokes represent the parts of a prepared message. They align toward a clear green outgoing arrow, expressing an explicit request or refusal with a coherent objective.

patterns.title: Cope Ahead: Rehearse Before the Difficult Moment
patterns.short_description: Prepare for a foreseeable challenge by choosing concrete responses and rehearsing yourself using them, including a fallback.
example_user_queries: I keep replaying a conversation that has not happened yet.
I want to prepare for a difficult appointment.
I know a particular moment will be hard and need a response ready.
I forget my plan when I feel under pressure.
How can I rehearse a boundary before a family conversation?
I need a fallback if I lose my words.
I want to practise coping rather than only imagining failure.
I do not make mental pictures but still want to rehearse.

visual_decision.reading: A gray route and a parallel ink route connect the present to a later point. A green detour represents a rehearsed fallback when a difficulty appears. The diagram expresses preparation, not a promised future result.

patterns.title: Opposite Action: Change an Unhelpful Action Urge
patterns.short_description: Check whether an emotional urge fits the situation, then practise a safe, deliberate alternative when changing that response would help.
example_user_queries: I want connection but keep avoiding safe social plans.
I feel an urge to hide after an ordinary mistake.
How can I choose a different action while the feeling is still present?
I need to check whether avoiding something is actually helping.
I want to take one safe step toward something I value.
I cannot tell whether to respond to the feeling or change my action.
I tried a different action once but still felt anxious.
I need an alternative to an urge that makes the situation harder.

visual_decision.reading: A shared ink starting point leads to a gray branch and a separate green branch in the other direction. The highlighted path represents a chosen safe alternative after checking whether it fits, not a rule that every urge must be reversed.

patterns.title: Self-Soothe: Build a Sensory Toolkit
patterns.short_description: Explore safe, accessible sensory experiences and keep a small set that offers comfort or steadiness during difficult moments.
example_user_queries: I feel braced after a difficult day and need some comfort.
I want a few sensory options that actually suit me.
Calming music makes me more irritated.
I need support while waiting for something I cannot resolve yet.
I want to build a simple comfort kit without buying special products.
How can I find a soothing option when scents are unsuitable?
I need less sensory input instead of another activity.
I tried something relaxing and nothing changed.

visual_decision.reading: Five separate outlined elements surround an open center. One green element marks a chosen sensory option; the other routes remain available without a requirement to use all senses.

patterns.title: Pros and Cons: Look Beyond the Immediate Urge
patterns.short_description: Compare the immediate and later effects of acting on an urge and choosing a specific alternative before deciding what to do next.
example_user_queries: I know an action may have costs but immediate relief feels more important.
I want to think before posting an angry public reply.
I keep overlooking what happens after I act on an urge.
How can I compare waiting with acting right now?
I want to admit the appeal of an urge without endorsing it.
I need a reminder of why I chose another response.
I want to compare short-term and longer-term consequences.
I am stuck making lists and need to identify what matters most.

visual_decision.reading: Four outlined quadrants hold both sides of two options. A green horizontal arrow beneath them extends the view beyond the immediate moment; no quadrant is marked as an automatic winner.

patterns.title: Validation and Self-Validation: Make Experience Understandable
patterns.short_description: Acknowledge an experience accurately and recognize what makes sense in context while preserving room for facts, limits, and change.
example_user_queries: I want someone to feel heard before I offer advice.
I judge myself for feeling the way I do.
How can I acknowledge a feeling without agreeing with a conclusion?
I rush to explain why someone should not be upset.
I want to understand an experience without inventing a motive.
I need to acknowledge frustration while keeping a boundary.
Kind statements sound false when I say them to myself.
How can I check that I understood another person accurately?

visual_decision.reading: An ink element is held within an open gray frame that represents context. A green echo beside it represents accurate acknowledgment while the open boundary leaves room for correction and change.

patterns.title: Radical Acceptance: Acknowledge What Is Here
patterns.short_description: Acknowledge a present fact you cannot change in this moment, make room for your response, and choose what remains possible.
example_user_queries: I keep arguing with something that has already happened.
I cannot change this fact right now and do not know how to respond.
I worry that accepting reality means approving of it.
I keep checking a cancellation as though it might disappear.
I want to acknowledge what happened without giving up on change.
I try to accept a situation and then reject it again.
I need a small everyday way to practise acceptance.
I want to distinguish a present fact from a prediction about the future.

visual_decision.reading: An ink block represents a fact already present. A green path begins beside it and moves forward, expressing a response possible from this reality without suggesting approval or erasure of the fact.
